01 / Full-bloom timing

A gradual shift toward earlier full bloom

Average full-bloom dates show a clear downward trend over time, suggesting earlier full bloom in recent decades. Despite substantial variation across stations and years, this shift is visible in both the full dataset and the Somei-yoshino records. Lower day-of-year values mean earlier bloom.

02 / Variation across places

Regional differences remain substantial

Full bloom is concentrated around days 90–110 , with earlier and later groups. Station-level views reveal variation that a national average can conceal.

03 / A consequential data decision

Which stations should define the modeling population?

Restricting analysis to stations with full-bloom observations in 2025 changes both geographic coverage and the amount of historical evidence.

All Somei-yoshino stations82 stations

5,161 valid historical full-bloom records

→
Stations observed in 202548 stations

3,477 valid historical full-bloom records

The restriction retains 67.4% of valid records and removes 34 stations and 1,684 records. These counts refer to full-bloom observations, not the paired interval dataset.

For discussion

Should we limit both training and test datasets to stations with records in 2025?

Only 48 of the 82 Somei-yoshino stations have full-bloom records in 2025. Restricting both datasets to these stations would leave 3,477 historical full-bloom records, compared with 5,161 across all stations. We need to decide whether to use this smaller station set for both training and testing.

Why are records missing at some weather stations from 2007 onward? JMA automated many weather stations between 2007 and 2009. Weather measurements continued, but cherry blossom observations ended at some stations because they required people to check the trees in person.

04 / Flowering → full bloom

Typically about one week, with a long upper tail

Among 5,142 Somei-yoshino records with both dates, the mean interval is 6.61 days and the median is 6 days. The middle half lies between 5 and 8 days; observed values range from 1 to 26 days.

04 / Purpose & implications

Using the interval to build a full-bloom baseline

The purpose of this interval analysis is to support a baseline model for the full bloom date. The 600°C rule predicts the flowering date. Adding an estimated interval gives a baseline prediction for the full bloom date.

Baseline full bloom date = predicted flowering date + estimated interval

Implications

The interval varies across both years and stations. Therefore:

  • Use interval data from a recent period, such as the past 10 years.
  • Use a different average interval for each station.

Note: an optional next step

The time from flowering to full bloom may also depend on factors such as temperature. We could explore these relationships and build a model. However, the main purpose of this interval analysis is to build the baseline, rather than a separate interval prediction model. We will explore this only if time allows.

Flowering date: the start of flowering. Full bloom date: the date when approximately 80% of the flowers are open. Interval: the number of days between these two dates.

05 / Differences in the interval

Both station and year matter

The two-way ANOVA shows that the interval between flowering and full bloom differs significantly across both stations and years (p < 0.001 for both).
